card.official_title: Reduce City Contractor Paperwork: Require Regular Meetings of Procurement Policy Board
card.plain_title: Change city contracting paperwork, approvals, and public hearings
card.put_on_ballot_by: Not identified in the official guide.
card.yes_means: A yes vote lets city boards simplify contractor questionnaires, expands delegated contract approvals, changes hearing requirements, and requires quarterly Procurement Policy Board meetings.
card.no_means: A no vote keeps the existing questionnaire, approval limits, hearing rules, and lack of a required Procurement Policy Board meeting schedule.

what_changes.today: All prospective contractors complete the same detailed questionnaire, maintained by the Mayor’s Office of Contract Services and Comptroller, regardless of contract value.
what_changes.if_passes: The Procurement Policy Board could reduce requirements for some contractors; the Franchise and Concession Review Committee would gain similar authority for franchises and concessions.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: Agencies contracting for direct services must hold public hearings on their draft annual contracting plans.
what_changes.if_passes: Draft-plan hearings would no longer be required, but agencies would still publish final annual plans.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: The Mayor’s Office cannot delegate approval of certain contracts over $5 million to agency chief contracting officers.
what_changes.if_passes: It could delegate those approvals too, with the agency commissioner’s approval.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: State law allows public comments instead of in-person hearings for certain higher-value contracts.
what_changes.if_passes: City law would make that option permanent, and the board could set the contract-value threshold for public comments starting October 1, 2030.
what_changes.label: fact

what_changes.today: The Procurement Policy Board has no required regular meeting schedule.
what_changes.if_passes: The board would have to meet at least every three months beginning January 1, 2027.
what_changes.label: fact

who_is_affected: Businesses and nonprofits seeking city contracts, including smaller contractors
City agencies and officials who approve contracts
People using contracted services such as shelters, job training, and youth programs
Residents who participate in contracting hearings and public comment periods

fiscal_impact.text: The official guide does not include a cost estimate.
fiscal_impact.label: fact

steelman_yes.headline: Trade-off case from the official summary: allow simpler paperwork for smaller contractors rather than require the same detailed questionnaire for every contract.
more_reasons: Another reason from the summary is allowing agency-level approval of more contracts while keeping commissioner approval.
The summary also establishes a regular meeting requirement for the board that sets contracting rules.

best_evidence.text: The board could reduce questionnaire requirements for smaller contractors or lower-value contracts.
best_evidence.label: fact

best_evidence.text: Delegation of the additional large-contract approvals would require approval from the agency commissioner.
best_evidence.label: fact

steelman_yes.who_it_helps: The analysis-based case centers on contractors eligible for simpler questionnaires and agencies receiving more approval flexibility.
steelman_yes.answer_to_other_side: The summary shows that removing draft-plan hearings would not eliminate the duty to publish final plans; public comments on certain contracts would also remain.

steelman_no.headline: Trade-off case from the official summary: keep required hearings on draft service plans rather than leave publication of final plans as the requirement.
more_reasons: Another reason from the summary is keeping a uniform questionnaire under the Mayor’s Office of Contract Services and Comptroller.
The summary also shows that rejection would preserve limits on delegating approval of certain contracts over $5 million.

best_evidence.text: The proposal removes required public hearings on draft annual plans for direct-service contracts.
best_evidence.label: fact

best_evidence.text: Current rules require the same detailed questionnaire regardless of contract value and restrict delegation for certain contracts over $5 million.
best_evidence.label: fact

steelman_no.who_it_helps: The analysis-based case centers on residents who want required draft-plan hearings and retention of existing review requirements.
steelman_no.answer_to_other_side: Simpler questionnaires are one part of a broader package; keeping current law would also preserve required draft-plan hearings and existing limits on delegated approvals.

crux.text: The central trade-off is greater contracting flexibility versus retaining existing review and participation requirements. The cases above are drawn from the official summary, not attributed to submitted supporting or opposing statements.

evidence.text: The proposal authorizes simpler questionnaires; the guide does not specify which questions would be removed.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: Hearings on draft service-contracting plans and public comments on individual higher-value contracts are separate requirements affected by the proposal.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: State law already allows public comments instead of in-person hearings for certain higher-value contracts.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.text: Except for the board’s meeting schedule and its authority to set the public-comment threshold, changes take effect upon certification of voter approval.
evidence.label: fact

turing_yes.reason: For a measure with no organized Yes statement, this fairly presents the strongest merits-based case available in the official summary: questionnaire requirements could be scaled for smaller or lower-value contractors, some approvals could be delegated with commissioner approval, and the board would have a regular meeting schedule. It could make the benefit of the meeting requirement clearer, but does not distort the case.

turing_no.reason: For a measure with no organized No statement, this fairly presents the central trade-offs: loss of required hearings on draft service plans, retention of a uniform questionnaire, and current limits on delegated approvals. Those are plausible merits-based reasons to reject the package, and the card notes that final plans would still be published and contract comments remain available.
